title: First insight into oral health misinformation in Jordan; an analysis of web content and information-seeking behaviors
screen_reason: Infodemiological content analysis of Arabic-language web pages retrieved for Jordan (2019-2023): 193 of 320 relevant pages (60.3%) were coded as containing oral health misinformation, where misinformation was defined as claims that defy the scientific consensus or lack current scientific evidence and validity was checked against authoritative sources (NIH, National Library of Medicine, PubMed Open Access 2015+, Google Scholar 2015+). That is a share of items judged false/unsupported against an external ground truth with a stated denominator, i.e. a CONTENT prevalence estimate. The paper's second strand (Google Trends interest over time and by governorate) is relative search interest, not a misinformation share.

estimates.country: Jordan (Google Advanced Search region set to Jordan, language Arabic; Google Trends region Jordan)
estimates.platform: Web pages (open web, retrieved via Google Trends top queries run through Google Advanced Search)
estimates.date: Web pages published 1 January 2019 to 31 December 2023; content analysis carried out February to August 2024
estimates.measure_type: % of Jordanian Arabic-language oral-health web pages that published oral health misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 193 (60.3%) of the 320 web pages included for content analysis (Table 3: Misinformation 193, Valid information 127, Total 320)
estimates.denominator: 320 Arabic-language web pages relevant to oral health, published/available in Jordan 2019-2023; retrieved by running 40 top Google Trends search queries (from four Arabic concepts: teeth, teeth with glottal stop, mouth, tongue) through Google Advanced Search restricted to Jordan and Arabic, extracting all result pages with Data Miner (704 retrieved) and screening for relevance
estimates.definition: Web page categorised as containing misinformation if its article carried claims that directly defy the scientific consensus or that lack current scientific evidence (criteria from Swire-Thompson and Lazer); e.g. 'drinking fluoridated water causes dental caries' (contradicts consensus) or 'drug Buspirone causes dry mouth' (lacks up-to-date evidence); validity checked against NIH, National Library of Medicine, PubMed Open Access (2015 and later), 'the American Academy' and Google Scholar (2015 and later)
estimates.misinfo_def: "This spread of information that defies the scientific consensus, or misinformation, became particularly pronounced during the COVID-19 pandemic"; operationally: "Examples of misinformation include claims that directly defy the scientific consensus or that lack current scientific evidence."
estimates.source_quote: Among the 320 web pages included for content analysis, 193 (60.3%) web pages were found to have oral health-related misinformation published in their articles.
estimates.page_loc: Results, p. 6 (first line); denominators in Table 3; also Abstract
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two blinded, trained investigators (BA, YA), both dental surgery interns, manually analysed every web page between February and August 2024; each page was dichotomised as containing misinformation or not, with detection guided by Swire-Thompson and Lazer's criteria and validity checks against NIH, NLM, PubMed Open Access (2015+), 'the American Academy' and Google Scholar (2015+). Outcomes from both investigators were compared with a conditional-formatting formula in Excel and 'Divergent analyses between the two investigators were revisited and further analyzed until a consensus was reached'. No kappa or percent-agreement statistic is reported. All identified misinformation content is listed per page in S6 File.
estimates.moderator_quote: In phase two, these refined queries were then run using Google Advanced Search, with parameters set as follows: the region was set to Jordan, the language was set to Arabic, and the time range was selected from January 1, 2019, to December 31, 2023. ... Arabic web pages that consisted of articles where the search term was explicitly mentioned in the body of the article were included. ... Web pages that were published in English, that were exclusively marketing or advertisement content, or did not mention the search term in the article were excluded.
estimates.notes: breadth coded 'misleading' (the broadest tier) because the numerator mixes consensus-defying claims with claims that merely 'lack current scientific evidence', so a not-yet-substantiated but not demonstrably false claim also counts. denom_selection=curated: the frame is a multi-issue keyword corpus built from Google Trends TOP queries, i.e. popularity-ranked and rank-truncated (40 search strategies), not a census of Jordanian oral-health pages. Note that explicitly advertising/marketing pages were EXCLUDED before coding, which likely removes some commercially motivated false claims (28 misinformation pages were still coded as having a 'financial' publisher interest). Denominator inconsistency to flag: the Abstract and Results use 320 relevant pages (Table 3 totals 320), but the S4 File caption says relevance screening yielded 333 web pages; 320 is used here because it is the denominator of the 60.3% and of every table. year=2023 is the last year of the corpus window (pages published 2019-2023); the retrieval and coding themselves ran February-August 2024. platform_norm=web_cross_platform because the units are articles on many different websites; 'Google Search' would be defensible since the sampling frame is Google Advanced Search result pages.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: (1) 'Publishers without a professional background published 185 web pages (95.9%) of the total misinformation-expressing web pages' - the denominator is the 193 misinformation pages, so this is the composition OF misinformation by publisher type, not the share of non-professional pages that are false; the correct-direction figure (185/293 non-professional pages = 63.1%) is derivable from Table 3 but is never stated and is a publisher subgroup rather than the headline prevalence, so I left it out. The matching professional figure would be 8/27 = 29.6%. An adjudicator wanting a source-subgroup row can take both from Table 3. (2) Dental-specialty shares of misinformation (oral medicine 52.3%, general dentistry 35.2%, periodontics 7.8%, cariology 3.1%, orthodontics 1.0%, pedodontics 0.5%) and publisher-interest shares (well-being journalism 77.2%, financial 14.5%, informational 5.7%, social 2.6%) and theme shares (dental 54.4%, lifestyle 23.8%, medical 11.4%, herbal 10.4%) - all have the 193 misinformation pages as denominator, i.e. within-misinformation composition, not prevalence. (3) Table 4's contextual distribution (causes 18.8%, home remedies 15.7%, treatment 15.5%, definition 12.5% ...) - shares of misinformation CONTENT categories inside the misinformation set; within-misinformation composition again. (4) Tables 5-7 (Google Trends popularity indices by year, by governorate and by region, all 0-100 relative-interest scores) - search interest, not a misinformation share, and the authors caution these 'represent relative search interests ... rather than absolute search volumes'. (5) No RECALL/EXPOSURE measure exists: the 'information-seeking behaviours' strand is entirely Google Trends, with no survey respondents. Judgement call for the adjudicator: platform_norm (web_cross_platform vs Google Search) and year (2023, end of corpus window, vs 2024, when retrieval and coding were done).

rob.design: Mixed-methods infodemiological content analysis. Sampling frame: four Arabic oral-health concepts entered in Google Trends (region Jordan, 1 Jan 2019-31 Dec 2023, all categories, web search); the top search queries (40 strategies, S1 File) were cleaned of duplicates/irrelevant items and re-run in Google Advanced Search (region Jordan, Arabic, same date range), results archived on Archive Today, and web pages extracted with Data Miner independently by two investigators and de-duplicated; 704 pages retrieved, 320 relevant pages analysed (S4 File says 333 after relevance screening - unexplained discrepancy). Browser cookies and history cleared to reduce personalisation. Coding: two blinded trained investigators (dental surgery interns) coded each page as containing misinformation or not between Feb and Aug 2024, using Swire-Thompson and Lazer criteria and checks against NIH/NLM/PubMed OA 2015+/Google Scholar 2015+; disagreements resolved by consensus; NO inter-rater reliability statistic reported. Statistics: Fisher's exact tests for validity by publisher interest/theme/background, Kruskal-Wallis for contextual and Google Trends comparisons (GraphPad Prism 10). Limitations acknowledged by the authors: Google Trends gives relative not absolute interest; no social-media analysis; Jordan-restricted retrieval may miss Arabic pages from other countries. Advertising/marketing-only pages were excluded before coding. All nine supporting data files are published with the paper.
rob.item6_quote: Each web page was categorized as either containing misinformation or not. Detection of misinformation was guided by the criteria established by Swire-Thompson and Lazer. Examples of misinformation include claims that directly defy the scientific consensus or that lack current scientific evidence. For example, the statement 'drinking fluoridated water causes dental caries' contradicts the scientific consensus, whereas the claim 'drug Buspirone causes dry mouth' lacks an up-to-date supporting evidence.
rob.item10_quote: Among the 320 web pages included for content analysis, 193 (60.3%) web pages were found to have oral health-related misinformation published in their articles.
